transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Lila Ramos (CTO, Peregrine), Samir Khan (Lead Eng), Nina Ortiz (Security), Alex Wu (Product)

Summary:
Quick live demo and 'cheatsheet' style walk through of Hosted API chat/text generation basics focusing on streaming, key parameters, and retry/backoff patterns. Covered console live tour for per-route metrics, and brief callout to Redwood Optimize tips for batching and cost. Discussed security requirements (KMS, audit logs) and next steps for pilot.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API usage model and simple API calls
- Streaming responses vs non-streaming
- Parameters: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop, stream config, token billing implications
- Idempotency, rate limits, retry/backoff patterns and example pseudo-code
- Console: token-level cost breakdown, per-route dashboards, trace links
- Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, caching, quantization guidance for embeddings/response caching
- Security: KMS integrations, data retention policy, SOC2

00:00 Maya: okay hi everybody thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, and with me is Owen who will run the demo; can you give a quick intro Owen?
00:08 Owen: yeah hi all, Owen Patel, Solutions Eng, I focus on performance and streaming behavior; today we'll do a short live walk through — start with the basic chat call, then streaming, then retries; if we run out of time we'll follow up with the notebook snippets
00:20 Lila: great, thanks; quick note we are evaluating for two product flows: clinician chat (low latency, HIPAA considerations) and patient summary generation (higher throughput but batchy)
00:32 Samir: timeline is ~Q4 pilot then decide on Dedicated vs Hosted depending on perf and compliance; question up front: do you support bringing our keys?
00:42 Maya: short answer yes for Private but on Hosted we have KMS integrations and customer-managed keys via our enterprise/private planes — we'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs after the call
00:53 Nina: please send us the audit log format, we need to show how records line up with our SIEM
00:58 Maya: noted, will share; Owen can you start with the API snippet?
01:03 Owen: sure, so simplest chat call — post to /v1/chat with messages payload. (slight pause) I'll paste the curl we usually show.
01:12 (screen share)
01:15 Owen: Example: 
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat 
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -d '{"model": "redwood-1.4-chat", "messages": [{"role":"system","content":"You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role":"user","content":"Summarize patient visit notes."}], "max_tokens": 400, "temperature": 0.2}'
01:41 Samir: quick q — how do you stream tokens? can we get partial results to show in our UI as they arrive?
01:49 Owen: yes, we support streaming via server-sent events. You flip stream:true and the connection yields deltas. Important to set smaller chunk sizes client-side to render smoothly, and watch for the final event that signals completion.
02:04 Owen: here's a Python SDK sketch: 
client.chat.stream(model='redwood-1.4-chat', messages=msgs, stream=True)
for chunk in stream: render(chunk.text)
02:18 Maya: two practical notes — streaming costs tokens the same as non-streaming (you pay for tokens produced), and you still get the same model quality; streaming just reduces perceived latency in UI.
02:30 Lila: okay, and what about token accounting for partials?
02:34 Owen: partial tokens not committed until model emits them — billing is per token generated at completion; however be mindful of prompt size (context tokens) which count towards usage.
02:44 Alex: if we want to preserve conversation context across sessions, what's the best approach?
02:49 Owen: you can persist the last N messages and resupply as context; Redwood also offers prefix caching and KV cache in Dedicated/Private which reduces context recompute — for Hosted we can recommend conservative context window sizes and use embeddings to fetch relevant context.
03:05 Samir: how about params — temperature/top_p/stopping? any defaults?
03:09 Owen: default temperature = 0.0 to 0.2 for deterministic clinical outputs, but for patient-facing summaries you can relax. top_p is supported; stop sequences we recommend explicit stop tokens to avoid trailing metadata. Also max_tokens should be budgeted — we gave an example with 400.
03:24 Owen: show retry patterns — e.g., idempotency_key header for safe retries on timeouts; hard vs soft errors: 5xx or rate-limit 429 handle differently.
03:34 Owen: pseudo code: 
- if 429 -> exponential backoff with jitter, retry up to N
- if 5xx -> retry with longer backoff, track idempotency_key to avoid double effects
- if client disconnect -> consider reconnect and resume streaming if you saved last event id
03:51 Samir: do you recommend client-side queueing? we have spikes when patients log in at shift change
03:56 Owen: yes, thin client-side queue and exponential backoff; server-side Redwood will return Retry-After headers when queuing; for spikes we can suggest Reserved burst capacity (Dedicated) or autoscaling policies on Dedicated; for Hosted we have rate limits per API key and recommend token buckets on client side.
04:16 Nina: security question — how long do you retain logs and transcripts on Hosted?
04:20 Maya: on Hosted default retention is 30 days for content logs; for enterprise we can configure retention windows and also support real-time forwarding to customer's SIEM; discuss offline later — we'll include retention matrix in the docs.
04:31 Owen: back to streaming failure modes — sometimes you get partial delta chunks then a socket close; pattern we recommend: client keeps last good chunk id, attempt a reconnect passing conversation state, and ask Redwood to continue; we surfaced this in our SDK with resume tokens but note that resume isn't perfect across model changes.
04:51 Samir: any known interoperability issues with mobile clients?
04:54 Owen: flaky mobile networks sometimes yield half-open connections; to mitigate use short keepalives, smaller streaming chunk thresholds, and graceful UI fallbacks with typed 'still thinking' ellipsis. Also server-side timeouts default to 60s but configurable for enterprise.
05:12 (brief crosstalk)
05:18 Owen: now the Console tour — I'll flip to Console. Top of Console, you can see per-route request/latency distribution, token-level cost graph, and model profile where we show 95th percentile latency per sequence length.
05:31 Owen: here's the per-route traces — click into a trace to see input messages, streaming events, and the kernel selection the runtime used (GPU type approx).
05:42 Alex: useful — can product see cost broken down by environment? we have staging vs prod budgets
05:46 Owen: yes, you can filter by API key labels and route tags; tag your keys by environment and Console will show cost by tag.
05:54 Maya: also Redwood Optimize will give suggestions if your workload shows long tails — like recommend batching or heavier quantization for response-only workloads; we can run a quick analyze on your traffic snapshot as part of the pilot.
06:10 Owen: demoing a quick stream — note how we surface partial tokens in the trace. 
06:18 (demo plays, some network lag)
06:30 Lila: I noticed the response came in two phases, what's that about?
06:33 Owen: that's usually prefix processing then generation — some models warm up KV cache; also Redwood's continuous batching might pack small requests and emit a first chunk quickly then rest after more decoding.
06:47 Samir: question on concurrency — what are realistic per-GPU qps numbers?
06:50 Owen: depends on model size and sequence length, but for redwood-1.4-chat with average ~200 output tokens, you can see mid-hundreds qps on a DGX-class setup; on Hosted we publish perf profiles in the model catalog — we'll share the link.
07:08 Samir: can you run a simple benchmark with our sample prompt?
07:11 Owen: yes, Owen: we can run a perf harness during the pilot; we'll need a representative prompt set and concurrency shape.
07:17 Maya: I'll note that as next step: prepare prompt set and schedule 48-hour pilot.
07:22 Nina: another security — SSO and RBAC — do you support SAML?
07:26 Maya: we do SAML SSO and RBAC for Console; will include tenant scoping docs and audit log format.
07:33 (walkthrough continues)
07:38 Owen: now a brief on retries and idempotency in streaming: you should include an idempotency_key even for non-mutating chat calls so if you have network retries you don't overspend or double-submit. We also provide a dry-run option for validation.
07:56 Alex: what's dry-run?
07:58 Owen: a validation endpoint that checks tokenization and estimated token cost without charging full generation; handy for client-side budgeting.
08:05 Samir: excellent. On billing: is there an overage protection or soft cap?
08:10 Maya: Console supports billing alerts and soft caps per API key; we can configure webhook notifications and auto-throttles.
08:18 Nina: For HIPAA we need BAA — do you have one?
08:21 Maya: Redwood offers BAAs for enterprise customers on Private or Dedicated; let's flag that for legal track — I'll bring our legal rep in the loop.
08:30 Lila: For pilot we're fine with hosted but need assurance on encryption-at-rest and in-flight and key management docs.
08:36 Maya: we'll send KMS and encryption docs and a short checklist for HIPAA readiness.
08:41 (short silence while demo continues)
08:48 Owen: final tip from Optimize: if your workload is mostly rephrasing or templated summaries, use a smaller chat variant for generation and a higher-quality model for hallucination-sensitive tasks; also enable prefix caching for repeated patient templates. That can cut token costs by 30-60% depending on repetitiveness.
09:08 Samir: real quick — how do we push updates to prompts safely? CI workflow?
09:12 Owen: use per-route versioning in Console, and canary rollouts; we have an API to pin traffic percentages across model versions so you can test 5% then 50% then cutover.
09:22 Alex: perfect.
09:24 Maya: let's do a quick recap and action items.
09:27 Maya: recap: we'll send the streaming cheatsheet, SOC2 and KMS docs, audit log format; Owen will scope pilot and perf harness; legal and Nina will follow up re: BAA/retention; Samir and team to drop representative prompts into the shared spreadsheet (link shared in chat).
09:44 Lila: timeline I'd say 2 weeks to gather prompts, 1 week to sign pilot T&Cs, then start 48-hour run — is that plausible?
09:52 Maya: yes that matches our typical cadence.
09:55 Owen: I'll also include sample retry pseudo-code and a small node/python streaming snippet in the follow up.
10:03 Maya: any final questions?
10:05 Nina: just please include a sample audit log event with field descriptions.
10:09 Maya: will do.
